# The question we will investigate

**Main question:** How do our choices about representing text change what we see?

Units 11 and 12 compared objects through distances. We now need to decide what
the measurements of a text document should be. Before making a map, we will
read texts, count words, choose weights, and check how much context is lost.

Use these notes during class and keep them for review. Every worked BBC example
is followed by a task on **a different corpus: SMS messages**. This transfer is
deliberate: short informal messages need not behave like news articles.

A **token** is one occurrence of a small piece of text produced by a splitting
rule. In this unit, think of it informally as a **word occurrence**: `tea tea
cake` contains three tokens, even though it has only two different word forms.
**Tokenisation** means splitting text into these units. We will examine the
precise splitting and filtering rules later; this first definition lets us
describe document length before studying those choices.

## Learning goals

- Define a document, a token, metadata and a document-term matrix (DTM).
- Explain how tokenisation and vocabulary filtering alter the data.
- Distinguish counts, relative frequencies and TF-IDF weights.
- Compare word clouds with ordered bars and interpret n-grams in context.
- Read directed bigram networks and use their paths to propose longer phrases
  that can be checked in the original texts.
- Keep a reproducible record of decisions and their consequences.

## What you need

**Prerequisites:** R indexing, tables, proportions, simple plots and matrices.
**R packages:** `ggplot2`, `knitr` and `rmarkdown`. The inspectable helpers in
`data/text_helpers.R` use base R; no specialist text-mining package is required.

Open the course folder (the folder containing these Rmd files and `data/`).
Keep a script called `13_my_text_lab.R`. Append an answer after each activity;
do not overwrite earlier results when changing a setting. A useful entry is
**prediction -> code -> output -> interpretation -> limitation**.

# Data and context

The guided corpus contains 250 **real BBC articles**, 50 in each of five topics.
Your activity corpus contains 240 **real SMS messages**, 120 labelled `ham`
(ordinary messages) and 120 `spam`. Exact text duplicates were removed before
sampling. The full downloaded archives contained 2,225 BBC articles and 5,574
SMS rows; after exact-text deduplication, 2,127 and 5,171 unique texts remained.

One complete article or message is one document. Sentences are temporary units
for extracting adjacent words; they will not become separate MDS points.

| Column | Meaning | Analytical role |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `document_id` | Unique retained document | Row label |
| `text` | Original complete text | Source of features |
| `category` | BBC topic or SMS label | Metadata; excluded from word features |
| `source_id` | Original file path or row | Traceability |
| `raw_tokens` | Baseline token count, calculated by the import helper | Derived document-length measure; not an original CSV column |

The files retain the original text. English ASCII-letter tokenisation below is
a simple baseline, not a language-independent linguistic parser. These older
corpora do not represent all present-day news or messaging.

```{r local-data}
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
source("data/text_helpers.R")
bbc <- load_text_docs("data/bbc_articles_250.csv")
sms <- load_text_docs("data/sms_messages_240.csv")
```


# Begin with documents, not with a cloud

Read a few articles before calculating summaries. Check identifiers, category
counts and length. The import helper creates `raw_tokens`: the **number of
baseline word tokens in each complete document**, counting repeated occurrences.
For this initial count it lowercases text, recognises English-letter sequences
with internal apostrophes, drops single-letter words and excludes numeric
tokens. It has not yet removed stopwords or applied a document-frequency filter.

Thus `raw_tokens` is a document-length measure, not a list of tokens or a count
of distinct words. It follows the stated rule rather than a universal definition
of a word. We will inspect and change that rule in the next section.

```{r bbc-audit, fig.cap="Each point is an article, not a word. Boxplots summarise article-length distributions."}
table(bbc$category)
summary(bbc$raw_tokens)
head(bbc[c("document_id", "category", "raw_tokens")])
# Read the full first article in the R console when discussing its context:
# cat(bbc$text[1])
ggplot(bbc, aes(category, raw_tokens)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, seed = 13),
             alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "BBC topic", y = "Baseline tokens per article")
```


**Reading the figure.** The vertical scale is document length. Different topics
can have different typical lengths, and documents in the same topic also vary.
A larger total word count in a group could reflect longer texts, more texts,
or both. Labels are useful for checking our map later, not for defining distance.

# Decide what becomes a token

Our `word_tokens()` function lowercases text, recognises letter sequences
with internal apostrophes, and discards single-letter words. Its optional
numeric-token rule retains digit sequences. Punctuation, emojis, URLs and
hyphens are not interpreted semantically; URL pieces can survive as words.
Inspect the function before treating its output as a complete description.

A **stopword list** removes selected common words. It is a modelling choice,
not an objective definition of useless language. Our short supplied list keeps
`no`, `not` and `never`. Check contractions and domain-specific expressions
before interpreting meaning or sentiment.

```{r cleaning, fig.cap="Corpus-level counts: a long article contributes more tokens than a short article."}
bbc_tokens <- word_tokens(bbc$text)
bbc_clean <- word_tokens(bbc$text, stop_words = course_stopwords)
raw_counts <- term_counts(bbc_tokens)
clean_counts <- term_counts(bbc_clean)
head(raw_counts, 10)
head(clean_counts, 10)
top_bars(setNames(clean_counts$count, clean_counts$term),
         "BBC: frequent retained words", ylab = "Token occurrences")
```


**Interpretation.** Removal changes both the vocabulary and the denominator of
later proportions. A term can become relatively frequent without gaining any
occurrences. Names, abbreviations and spelling variants remain separate forms.

**Stemming** reduces related forms to a common stem (possibly not a word).
**Lemmatisation** aims at dictionary forms using linguistic information. Neither
is applied in the core analysis. For example, combining `run` and `running`
changes a column definition; a guessed suffix rule is not reliable lemmatisation.

# From words to a common document-term matrix

Let $C_{it}$ count term $t$ in document $i$. Every row uses the **same vocabulary**.
Rows are documents and columns are terms; metadata never enter this matrix.
A zero means no retained occurrence, not missing information. Word order has
been discarded: this is a **bag-of-words** representation.

```{r tiny-dtm}
toy <- c("tea tea cake", "tea bread", "bread cake")
toy_C <- make_dtm(word_tokens(toy), c("D1", "D2", "D3"), min_df = 1)
toy_C
bbc_C <- make_dtm(bbc_clean, bbc$document_id, min_df = 2)
c(documents = nrow(bbc_C), terms = ncol(bbc_C),
  zero_fraction = mean(bbc_C == 0), empty_rows = sum(rowSums(bbc_C) == 0))
```


**Document frequency** $df_t=\sum_i I(C_{it}>0)$ counts documents containing a
term, not its total occurrences. The threshold `min_df=2` retains terms found
in at least two documents. This reduces isolated spellings and singleton terms,
but may discard meaningful rare words. It is not a statistical significance rule.

```{r small-heatmap, fig.cap="Counts for ten selected articles and ten frequent terms. Rows and columns are not clustered or standardised."}
chosen_terms <- head(names(sort(colSums(bbc_C), decreasing = TRUE)), 10)
small <- bbc_C[seq(1, 250, length.out = 10), chosen_terms]
heatmap(small, Rowv = NA, Colv = NA, scale = "none",
        margins = c(7, 8), col = hcl.colors(20, "Blues 3"))
```

# Frequent and distinctive are different questions

Work with **one corpus at a time**, after choosing its stopwords and retained
vocabulary and excluding documents that have no retained terms. Before using
the formula, define its ingredients:

- $N$ is the number of **retained documents** in that corpus. The document
  index is $i=1,\ldots,N$; here one document is one complete article or SMS.
- $V$ is the number of **distinct retained terms** in the common vocabulary.
  A term is a word form used as a matrix column. The index $t=1,\ldots,V$
  identifies the term of interest; $s$ is another index that runs through the
  same vocabulary when we sum over terms.
- $C_{it}$ is the **number of occurrences** of term $t$ in document $i$.
  This is a cell of the document-term count matrix $C$; repetitions count.
- $L_i=\sum_{s=1}^{V}C_{is}$ is the total number of **retained token occurrences**
  in document $i$. It is positive for every retained document. It generally
  differs from `raw_tokens`, which was calculated before stopword removal
  and vocabulary filtering.
- $I(C_{it}>0)$ is an **indicator**: it equals 1 if document $i$ contains at
  least one occurrence of term $t$, and 0 otherwise.

We can now define four related quantities:

\[
p_{it}=\frac{C_{it}}{L_i},\qquad
df_t=\sum_{i=1}^{N}I(C_{it}>0),
\]

\[
idf_t=\log\left(\frac{N}{df_t}\right),\qquad
W_{it}=p_{it}\,idf_t.
\]

1. **Term frequency (TF), $p_{it}$:** the proportion of retained tokens in
   document $i$ that are term $t$. The proportions sum to one within each
   document. Here TF means a proportion, not a raw count.
2. **Document frequency, $df_t$:** the number of retained documents containing
   term $t$. Each document contributes at most one, however often it repeats
   the term. For a retained term, $1\leq df_t\leq N$.
3. **Inverse document frequency (IDF), $idf_t$:** the natural logarithm of
   $N/df_t$. It is a corpus-level weight, shared by all documents for that
   term. A term appearing in fewer documents receives a larger IDF; a term
   appearing in every document has $idf_t=\log(1)=0$.
4. **TF-IDF, $W_{it}$:** the product of the within-document proportion and the
   corpus-level IDF. The matrix $W$ has the same document rows and term columns
   as $C$, but its entries are weights rather than counts. A large value
   identifies a term that is relatively frequent in this document and not
   widespread across the corpus; it does not establish universal importance.

**A constructed numerical example.** Suppose a term occurs 4 times among
100 retained tokens in one document and occurs in 10 of the corpus's 50
retained documents. Its TF is $4/100=0.04$, its document frequency is 10,
its IDF is $\log(50/10)=\log(5)$, and its TF-IDF in that document is
$0.04\log(5)\approx 0.0644$. The four occurrences count four times for TF,
but this document contributes only one to document frequency. These numbers
illustrate the formula; they are not a measured BBC result.

We use the natural logarithm and no additive smoothing. Software defaults
differ, so report this convention and the retained-token denominator.
The same count can get different weights in different corpora. If every term
appears in every document, all IDFs are zero; a zero TF-IDF vector cannot be
normalised for cosine comparisons.

Before normalising, remove and report empty rows once. Use that common document
set for all representations. `prepare_text()` performs this check and stops on
zero TF-IDF norms rather than inventing values.

```{r weights, fig.cap="Article-level TF-IDF: a high bar means distinctive within this retained BBC corpus, not universally important."}
demo <- prepare_text(bbc)
lab <- prepare_text(sms)
demo$removed
lab$removed
R_bbc <- demo$representation
R_sms <- lab$representation
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(R_bbc$P) - 1) < 1e-12))
selected_id <- rownames(R_bbc$C)[1]
profile <- data.frame(term = colnames(R_bbc$C),
                      count = R_bbc$C[selected_id, ],
                      tf = R_bbc$P[selected_id, ], idf = R_bbc$idf,
                      tfidf = R_bbc$W[selected_id, ])
head(profile[order(-profile$tfidf), ], 10)
top_bars(setNames(profile$tfidf, profile$term),
         "One BBC article: distinctive terms", ylab = "TF-IDF")
```

# A word cloud needs a named quantity

For a topic-level summary, we will average **article-level** TF-IDF values,
including zeros for articles without the term. This gives articles equal
weight. It differs from pooling tokens, where long articles contribute more.

```{r cloud-and-bars, fig.cap="Bars and cloud use the same twenty terms and weights. Cloud position is a layout choice, not a semantic coordinate."}
business <- demo$docs$category == "business"
topic_weights <- colMeans(R_bbc$W[business, , drop = FALSE])
shown <- head(sort(topic_weights, decreasing = TRUE), 20)
top_bars(shown, "Business: mean article TF-IDF", n = 20,
         ylab = "Mean TF-IDF, including zeros")
draw_cloud(shown, n = 20, seed = 13)
```


**Reading the figures.** Bars have a common baseline and support direct
comparisons. In the cloud, font size encodes weight, but rendered area also
depends on word length. Position, proximity and direction have no analytic
meaning. The supplied packing helper uses font size proportional to an affine
function of square-root weight; it does not promise area-proportional encoding.
A cloud is an overview, not a substitute for numerical comparison.

# Recover a little order with n-grams

A bigram is a pair of adjacent tokens; a trigram has three. Extract them
**before** deleting words, and avoid crossing sentence or document boundaries.
Only afterwards filter n-grams containing stopwords. Otherwise removing `of`
from the constructed phrase `bank of england` would invent `bank england`.
The phrase is a teaching illustration, not an extracted BBC quotation.

```{r bigrams, fig.cap="Bigrams are adjacent retained word sequences from within approximate sentence boundaries."}
phrase <- "bank of england"
sentence_ngrams(phrase, filter_stop = FALSE)
word_tokens(phrase, stop_words = course_stopwords)
bbc_bigrams <- lapply(bbc$text, sentence_ngrams)
bigram_counts <- term_counts(bbc_bigrams)
top_bars(setNames(bigram_counts$count, bigram_counts$term),
         "BBC: retained adjacent bigrams", ylab = "Bigram occurrences")
```


Our sentence splitter is punctuation-based; abbreviations and unusual SMS
punctuation can defeat it. The baseline word rule also ignores punctuation
inside a sentence. Read contextual examples before treating any pair as a
linguistically validated expression. Same-document co-occurrence is a different
relationship from adjacency and can connect words many sentences apart.


## From bigram counts to a directed word network

The bigram table also defines a **directed network**:

- A **node** is a distinct word form, not an individual token occurrence.
- An **arrow** from word $a$ to word $b$ means that $b$ follows $a$ in at
  least one extracted bigram. The reverse order would be a different arrow.
- The **edge weight** is the number of occurrences of that ordered pair
  across the corpus. Thicker arrows represent more occurrences. A separate
  `documents` column counts how many different texts contain the pair.

The network retains the within-sentence extraction and stopword rules above.
It is an adjacency network, not a same-document co-occurrence network and
not a diagram of causal effects.

```{r bbc-bigram-network, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="BBC directed bigram network. Arrow width encodes occurrences. Shown: the three largest components with at least three words, after retaining at most forty non-self bigrams occurring at least ten times. Panels separate disconnected parts of this filtered graph."}
bbc_edges <- bigram_edges(bbc_bigrams, min_count = 10, top_n = 40)
head(bbc_edges)
bbc_network <- plot_bigram_network(bbc_edges, max_components = 3,
                                   title = "BBC: which words follow which?")
bbc_network$plot
```

**Reading the network.** Follow the arrowheads to read order. Several outgoing
arrows from `mr` show alternative continuations of a reporting convention;
this hub need not represent the most important topic. Other components suggest
names, multiword expressions or source-attribution patterns. These are starting
points for reading the articles, not automatically discovered topics.

To keep labels readable, the display selects frequent edges, omits repeated-word
self-loops, and shows only the three largest components of at least three nodes.
A component is a set connected when arrow direction is ignored. The original
bigram table is unchanged. A missing edge or disconnected panel can be a
consequence of the display filter; it does not prove absence from the full
corpus. The layout separates labels: geometric distance and edge crossings
have no semantic meaning. All plotting code is in the supplied helper file;
no extra R package is required.

## Let paths suggest longer n-grams, then verify them

A directed path $a\to b\to c$ suggests the candidate trigram `a b c`.
But its two edges may come from different sentences or different documents:
their presence does **not** establish that all three words occurred together.
Even if both edges are frequent, the longer phrase can be absent. Extract
trigrams from the original texts to answer that question.

```{r network-to-trigrams}
candidates <- candidate_trigrams(bbc_network$edges)
path_check <- verify_phrases(candidates, bbc$text, n = 3)
knitr::kable(path_check, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Candidate three-word paths and their actual within-sentence trigram counts.")
```

**Interpretation.** The table contains both observed phrases and candidates
with count zero. The graph is therefore useful for proposing expressions;
the ordered source tokens decide whether those expressions really occur.
Compare the two-edge paths with the longer name/reporting sequences visible
in the other components. A path with three arrows suggests four words:

```{r network-to-four-grams}
verify_phrases("actor jamie foxx actress", bbc$text, n = 4)
```

This four-gram is checked as an actual sequence, rather than inferred by
multiplying edge weights or taking their minimum. Bigram weights alone do
not determine trigram or four-gram frequencies. Longer n-grams retain more
context but usually have less support. Compare the count of an expression
with the number of source documents containing it before calling it a
general pattern. Changing an edge threshold can also break a visible path
without changing any original text.

# Sensitivity: a threshold changes what can be represented

The document-frequency threshold is part of the feature definition. Compare
BBC thresholds before choosing the more attractive plot.

```{r thresholds}
bbc_df5 <- make_dtm(bbc_clean, bbc$document_id, min_df = 5)
data.frame(min_df = c(2,5),
           vocabulary = c(ncol(bbc_C), ncol(bbc_df5)),
           empty = c(sum(rowSums(bbc_C)==0), sum(rowSums(bbc_df5)==0)))
```

# Bring the choices together

Before moving to distances, keep the document IDs, feature definitions and
weights together. A visually distinctive word may be a name, a formatting
artifact or a rare spelling; an appealing cloud does not validate the pipeline.

# Check your understanding

**Q1.** A term occurs ten times in one document and once in each of ten other
documents. What are its total count and document frequency?

**Q2.** Why can a word have a positive count but zero TF-IDF?

**Q3.** Does proximity in a word cloud imply semantic similarity?

**Q4.** Why retain complete messages as rows even when extracting sentence-level n-grams?

**Q5.** If both `a b` and `b c` occur in the corpus, must `a b c` occur?
How would you check rather than infer it from the network?

# Take-home messages

- A corpus is a collection of defined observational units, not just a bag of files.
- Preprocessing changes the variables; record the choices and inspect original texts.
- Counts, proportions and TF-IDF answer different questions.
- A word cloud needs explicit weights and does not supply a semantic geometry.
- Adjacent n-grams must be extracted before word deletion; verify their context.
- Directed bigram paths suggest longer phrases but cannot establish their
  presence or frequency. Check the original ordered tokens.
- Empty profiles must be handled explicitly before comparing documents.

  Greene and Cunningham (2006), ICML. Original article copyright remains BBC;
  the distributor specifies non-commercial and research use.
- [SMS Spam Collection](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/228/sms+spam+collection).
  Almeida and Hidalgo (2011), UCI, DOI 10.24432/C5CC84; CC BY 4.0.
- Silge and Robinson, [Text Mining with R](https://www.tidytextmining.com/):
  word frequencies, TF-IDF and n-grams.
- R documentation: [classical MDS](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/cmdscale.html)
  and [correspondence analysis](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/MASS/html/corresp.html).

See `data/text_corpora_sources.txt` and `data/text_corpora_manifest.json` for
selection, deduplication, source identifiers, seeds and file hashes. The supplied
CSVs are fixed classroom inputs. Both are balanced teaching subsets, not
estimates of real category prevalence. No download occurs while knitting.

# Reproducibility information

The worked examples and the separate instructor solutions were executed and
rendered when prepared. Activity starter chunks are intentionally unevaluated:
copy them to your own script or enable them after completing the instructions.
The following records the versions used for this rendering.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
